title: Primary Function of the Shaft Assembly
learningObjectives: Identify the shaft assembly's role in the production system.
student: State the primary structural and mechanical function of the shaft assembly.
instructor: The shaft distributes torque and mechanical power among multiple gear-driven stations while the bearings support and align the rotating shaft.

title: Applied Torsional Loads
learningObjectives: Identify the external actions included in the torsion model.
student: Identify the external mechanical loads relevant to the base torsion analysis.
instructor: The relevant loads are the applied torques TB, TC, TD, and TF at the four gear locations. Gear weights and transverse gear forces are excluded from the base torsion model.
gradingNotes: Students should distinguish torque from force and power.

title: Bearing Roles and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Distinguish radial support from torsional restraint.
student: Describe the mechanical role of bearings A and E in the simplified model.
instructor: The bearings restrain transverse motion and support the shaft while permitting rotation. Ideal frictionless bearings do not supply reaction torque about the shaft axis.

title: Torque Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace torque transfer through a multi-station shaft.
student: Trace how torque is transmitted through the shaft from one gear station to another.
instructor: Each gear adds or removes torque. The internal torque in any segment equals the algebraic sum of the external torques on one side of a cut through that segment.

title: Predicting the Governing Segment
learningObjectives: Predict how the governing segment will be identified.
student: Before calculating, explain how the governing solid-shaft segment will be identified.
instructor: Because every solid-shaft segment has the same diameter, the segment with the largest absolute internal torque has the largest maximum torsional shear stress and governs.

title: Parameters Controlling the Design
learningObjectives: Identify the inputs controlling shaft stress and wall thickness.
student: Identify the parameters that control solid-shaft shear stress and tubular wall thickness. Explain whether the segment lengths affect the base stress calculation.
instructor: Applied torques, shaft outer diameter, inner diameter or wall thickness, polar moment of inertia, and allowable shear stress control the design. Segment lengths describe the geometry and support optional angle-of-twist work, but they do not affect shear stress under Saint-Venant torsion.

title: Student-Generated Shaft Idealization
learningObjectives: Create a multi-torque shaft model before viewing the reference figure.
student: Before using the reference figure, draw a simplified shaft model showing points A through F, gear torques and directions, bearing locations, shaft segments, and shaft diameter. Establish a positive torque sign convention.
instructor: A correct model idealizes the assembly as a circular shaft with concentrated torques at B, C, D, and F and ideal rotation-permitting bearings at A and E. Torque arrows and the positive sign convention must be unambiguous.
gradingNotes: Students should attempt the model before seeing the instructor idealization.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the torsion model.
student: State the assumptions used in the base torsion model.
instructor: Assume a circular prismatic shaft, homogeneous linearly elastic material, concentrated static torques, ideal bearings that do not resist shaft-axis torque, small deformation, and Saint-Venant torsion. Neglect transverse gear forces, bending, warping restraint, and local stress concentrations.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan a complete segment-stress and sizing analysis.
student: Outline the calculation sequence before substituting numbers.
instructor: Choose a torque sign convention; verify overall torque equilibrium; cut each shaft segment and determine internal torque; construct the torque diagram; calculate solid-shaft shear stress; identify the governing torque; size the tubular shaft; round wall thickness upward to the available increment; and verify the selected thickness.

title: Torque Sign Convention and Overall Equilibrium
student: Select a positive torque direction and verify overall torque equilibrium for the assigned gear torques.
instructor: Using the signs supplied with the assignment, ΣT = TB + TC + TD + TF = {{gear_torque_sum_kNm}} kN·m. {{gear_equilibrium_assessment}}

title: Internal Torque in Each Segment
learningObjectives: Calculate internal torque throughout a multi-load shaft.
student: Determine the signed internal torque in segments AB, BC, CD, DE, and EF. Also report each magnitude.
instructor:
Using cuts and the assigned sign convention: TAB = {{gear_T_AB_kNm}} kN·m, TBC = {{gear_T_BC_kNm}} kN·m, TCD = {{gear_T_CD_kNm}} kN·m, TDE = {{gear_T_DE_kNm}} kN·m, and TEF = {{gear_T_EF_kNm}} kN·m.

The corresponding magnitudes are {{gear_abs_T_AB_kNm}}, {{gear_abs_T_BC_kNm}}, {{gear_abs_T_CD_kNm}}, {{gear_abs_T_DE_kNm}}, and {{gear_abs_T_EF_kNm}} kN·m.
commonMistakes: Do not replace the cumulative algebraic sum with the nearest applied gear torque.

title: Internal Torque Diagram
learningObjectives: Construct and interpret an internal torque diagram.
student: Construct the internal torque diagram along A-F and label the torque jump at every gear.
instructor: The diagram is {{gear_T_AB_kNm}} kN·m on AB, then changes to {{gear_T_BC_kNm}} on BC, {{gear_T_CD_kNm}} on CD, {{gear_T_DE_kNm}} on DE, and {{gear_T_EF_kNm}} kN·m on EF. Each jump equals the signed applied torque at that gear. Bearing E creates no jump.

title: Maximum Shear Stress in the Solid Shaft
learningObjectives: Calculate maximum torsional shear stress in every segment.
student: For the assigned solid-shaft diameter, calculate the maximum torsional shear stress in every segment using τmax = 16|T|/(πd3).
instructor: The segment stresses are τAB = {{gear_tau_AB_MPa}} MPa, τBC = {{gear_tau_BC_MPa}} MPa, τCD = {{gear_tau_CD_MPa}} MPa, τDE = {{gear_tau_DE_MPa}} MPa, and τEF = {{gear_tau_EF_MPa}} MPa.
commonMistakes: Convert kN·m to N·mm before using millimeter section dimensions.

title: Governing Shaft Segment
learningObjectives: Identify the segment controlling the tubular-shaft design.
student: Identify the governing segment or segments and explain why they control the tubular-shaft design.
instructor: {{gear_governing_segments}} {{gear_governing_verb}} with an internal torque magnitude of {{gear_governing_torque_kNm}} kN·m. The governing location carries the largest absolute internal torque, and the solid-shaft diameter is uniform.

title: Tubular-Shaft Sizing Equation
learningObjectives: Derive the allowable-stress equation for a hollow circular shaft.
student: Starting from τ = Tc/J, derive the equation for the maximum permissible tubular-shaft inner diameter.

title: Minimum Tubular Wall Thickness
learningObjectives: Select a manufacturable wall thickness from a theoretical minimum.
student: Determine the theoretical minimum tubular wall thickness and select the smallest thickness available in the assigned increment. Explain the rounding direction.
instructor: tmin = (Do - Di,max)/2 = {{gear_t_min_mm}} mm. Round upward to the assigned increment, giving {{gear_t_selected_mm}} mm. The corresponding selected inner diameter is {{gear_D_i_selected_mm}} mm.

title: Selected-Thickness Verification
student: Recalculate the maximum shear stress using the selected wall thickness and determine the allowable-stress utilization.
instructor: The selected wall gives τmax = {{gear_tau_selected_MPa}} MPa and utilization τmax/τallow = {{gear_utilization}}. {{gear_thickness_assessment}}

title: Bearing E and Equal Adjacent Torques
learningObjectives: Explain why an ideal bearing does not change internal torque.
student: Explain why bearing E does not create a jump in the torque diagram and why segments DE and EF carry the same torque.
instructor: An ideal bearing does not apply torque about the shaft axis. Internal torque is therefore unchanged across E, so DE and EF carry the same signed internal torque until the external torque at F is applied.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
student: Provide a concise recommendation for the tubular shaft and identify important limitations of the base model.
instructor:
{{gear_recommendation}}

Detailed design must additionally evaluate bending from gear forces, combined stress, fatigue, keyways and shoulders, stress concentrations, angular twist, critical speed, bearing loads, manufacturing tolerances, and applicable standards.
gradingNotes: Students should not claim full machine safety from the pure-torsion calculation alone.
